title: Too Good to Be True
realOrConstructed: Real people and evidence in an imagined courtroom
bigUnderstanding: Who made a claim, and what they wanted, shapes what they say. The Virginia Company needed money and settlers, so it sold Virginia as paradise; the people who actually went told a very different story. The gap between the ad and reality cost lives. Quietly builds the habit Abi needs for modern ads and influencers: who's paying, what do they want me to do, who was actually there? Also sets up the investor pressure in the Jamestown simulation.

opening.intro: Order in the court! The families of Jamestown settlers say the Virginia Company lured people to their deaths with fake ads. The Company says Virginia is wonderful and the settlers ruined it. You're the judge.

cards.label: The charge
cards.text: The families: the Company promised paradise to raise money. People believed it, went, and died.

cards.label: The defense
cards.text: The Company: Virginia is rich. The settlers were lazy, quarrelsome, and hit by a hurricane. Not our fault.

cards.label: Your court
cards.text: Call witnesses. Examine exhibits. Ask anything. Witnesses only know what they saw, and every one of them wants something.

cards.label: How to win
cards.text: Deliver your ruling: who told the truth, why the other side said what it did, and 3 pieces of evidence that prove it.

opening.prompt: Who do you call first, Your Honor?

facilitatorNotes: COURTROOM FORMAT. You are the court clerk (brief, dry, a little theatrical) and you play every witness. Abi is the judge and runs the hearing: she calls witnesses, asks questions, examines exhibits, and rules. Keep each witness answer to 1–3 sentences in a distinct voice.

WITNESSES (call examine for the matching evidence when their testimony covers it):
- Robert Johnson, Company member who wrote the 1609 pamphlet (real). Enthusiastic salesman. Never went to Virginia. Covers: pamphlet. If pressed on whether he's been there, he squirms.
- Sir Thomas Smythe, the Company's treasurer (real). Smooth, polite, always has an excuse: hurricane, lazy settlers, bad luck. Covers: company_money, orders_1606, true_declaration, lottery. Never admits the ads were exaggerated unless Abi corners him with evidence.
- Captain John Smith (real). Blunt, boastful, furious at the Company and at the gentlemen. Covers: smith_letter, who_came, fools_gold.
- George Percy (real). Gentleman colonist who saw the sickness. Serious, a bit dramatic. Covers: percy, death_count.
- A gold refiner from the 1608 supply ship (INVENTED, say so if asked). Sheepish. Covers: fools_gold.
Exhibits (documents and data, no witness needed): powhatan_food, drought, plus any document above.
Witnesses can only testify to what they saw or wrote. Each has a motive; let it show so Abi can catch it. If Abi asks a witness about something they couldn't know, they say so.
A real trial like this never happened. The people, documents and facts are real, and testimony is built from what they actually wrote or did. Say so plainly if asked, and at the end.

This is a SOLVED case: the evidence clearly shows the Company oversold Virginia because it needed money and settlers. The settlers weren't blameless either (many gentlemen refused to work), and a sharp answer can include that.
The quotes are real 1600s writing put in modern words. If she asks, say they're modernized and that the originals use old spelling.
Keep it funny where the hype is ridiculous (shiploads of shiny dirt sent home as gold).

Do NOT mention modern ads or influencers during the case, and never suggest Abi personally falls for ads. After closing, add ONE short sentence connecting to today, like: 'Same trick still works: ask who's paying and what they want you to do.' Then offer to save a question about modern ads or influencers to her Wonder List if she seems interested.

The Powhatan appear in these sources through English eyes. If it comes up, point out that the English writers had their own reasons for how they described Native people, which is the same skill she's using.
Pin real events to her timeline as they come up.
Abi should discover the judge's key questions herself: Were you there? Who paid you? What do you want people to believe? Teach 'bias' and 'propaganda' only after she's found the idea.
justInTimeConcepts: Primary source: written by someone who was there, at the time.
Bias: a reason a source might lean one way.
Motive: who benefits if you believe this?
Propaganda: messages made to persuade, not to inform.
Investors and shares: people put money in hoping to get more back.
scaffolds: Ask each witness: were you actually in Virginia?
Ask the treasurer: how does the Company make money?
Who did the ads bring over, and what happened to them?
completion: Abi has heard or examined at least 3 pieces of evidence and delivered her ruling in her own words: who told the truth, why the other side said what it did, and at least 3 supporting pieces of evidence.

endReveal.concept: Source reliability and motive: ask who made a claim, whether they were there, and what they wanted. Messages built to persuade are called propaganda.

data.question: The ads said Virginia was paradise. The settlers said it was a nightmare. Who was telling the truth, and why would anyone say otherwise?
data.winCondition: Deliver your ruling: who told the truth, why the other side said what it did, and 3 pieces of evidence that prove it.
data.trueExplanation: The settlers' accounts are more reliable: they were there, and their hardship is confirmed by death counts. The Virginia Company oversold Virginia because it needed investors' money and settlers; it profited only if people believed. The hype attracted the wrong people (gentlemen and gold-seekers expecting easy riches), which made things worse. When disaster struck, the Company blamed the settlers and the weather and kept advertising. Strong answers also note the settlers weren't blameless (many refused to work) and that the land was rich for people who knew how to live there, like the Powhatan.

evidence.label: The 1609 pamphlet (Nova Britannia)
evidence.result: Written in London by Robert Johnson, a Company member who never went to Virginia. It praises rich soil, a healthy climate and endless resources, and urges readers to buy shares. Its goal: raise money and recruits.

evidence.label: How the Virginia Company made money
evidence.result: Investors bought shares. The Company made money only if Virginia produced something valuable to sell: gold, goods, or crops. For years, it produced almost nothing. It always needed new money from new believers.

evidence.label: The Company's orders to the first colonists (1606)
evidence.result: Find gold and other minerals. Find a river route to the Pacific Ocean (and on to Asian trade). Keep the colony well defended. Profit first.

evidence.label: Who actually signed up
evidence.result: Of the first 104 men and boys, about a third were listed as 'gentlemen,' men who didn't do manual work. Later ships brought goldsmiths and refiners to process the gold everyone expected. Very few farmers.

evidence.label: George Percy's account (1607)
evidence.result: A gentleman colonist who was there. In modern words: men died of swellings, fevers and stomach sickness, sometimes several a day; their only drink was salty, slimy river water; they were starving. He was a gentleman from a powerful family who wanted the colony to succeed, so he had no reason to make it look worse than it was.

evidence.label: John Smith's letter to the Company (1608)
evidence.result: Smith, who ran the colony for a while, wrote back angrily (in modern words): send me 30 carpenters, farmers, fishermen, blacksmiths and masons rather than a thousand of the kind we have. He complained the Company cared more about gold than survival.

evidence.label: The great gold rush of 1608
evidence.result: Colonists spent weeks digging glittery dirt and loaded a ship with it for London. Experts there tested it: worthless. Likely iron pyrite, 'fool's gold.' Meanwhile, the fields went unplanted.

evidence.label: How many survived
evidence.result: Of the 104 who landed in 1607, about 38 were alive when the first supply ship came in January 1608. In the 'Starving Time' winter of 1609–1610, roughly 500 colonists fell to about 60.

evidence.label: The Company's 1610 report after the Starving Time
evidence.result: The Company's official explanation blamed a hurricane, lazy and quarrelsome colonists, and bad luck. It insisted Virginia itself was still wonderful and kept recruiting.

evidence.label: How the Company kept raising money
evidence.result: When investors got nervous, the Company was allowed to run lotteries in England, starting in 1612, to raise money. More ads, more promises.

evidence.label: Did anyone in Virginia have plenty of food?
evidence.result: Yes. The Powhatan grew corn, beans and squash, fished and hunted, and stored food for winter. The land could feed people who knew how to live there. The English often traded for their corn, or took it.

evidence.label: Tree-ring data for 1606–1612
evidence.result: Tree rings show the driest seven years in about 770 years in that region. Even skilled farmers had bad harvests. Not something the ads mentioned.

theories.theory: The Company oversold Virginia to get money and settlers
The settlers exaggerated and just complained
Virginia was great; the settlers were just lazy
Both: oversold by the Company, made worse by the wrong people and bad choices
